description: Innovating cabbage production and making kimchi production more efficient.
summary: Kimchi is a map-based decision-support dashboard for farmers on limited irrigation. A farmer picks or draws a field, and Kimchi pulls live and historical NASA data for four factors: water balance, temperature (heat extremes and accumulated heat), soil moisture and crop condition. For each factor it shows how this season compares with 1991–2020, where the risk is on the map, how often it has recurred since 1981, and whether it is getting worse. It combines this with the farmer's own records (crops, irrigation, nitrogen, yield, well capacity, water allocation, priorities) to suggest the top 3 actions, each with visible evidence, benefits, risks and information gaps. It also compares the current rotation with alternatives (continuous corn, corn–sorghum, corn–winter wheat) over the same weather years. Our demo is an irrigated corn pivot in the Sheridan 6 water-conservation area of western Kansas, above the declining Ogallala aquifer. The tool supports farmer judgement and never replaces it: every recommendation ends with "Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting."
details:
Project details

What it does
- Four factors, four questions each. For each factor the dashboard shows:
- this season vs normal, in plain words with °F and inches;
- where the risk is, on a field view of satellite greenness and a regional NASA weather grid, with a time slider from 1981;
- how often it happens ("28 of 35 seasons");
- whether it is getting worse (shown only when there are at least 30 years of data).
- Top 3 actions from 12 sourced actions, ranked by a transparent score shown on every card: severity × farmer priority × evidence strength × timing. Each card starts collapsed (problem and a bold result) and expands to a chart and plain explanation.
- Rotation comparison: the current rotation plus at least 2 alternatives, each with how often it ran short of water, heat at pollination and months with little green cover. Each also lists why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, risks and unknowns. A "what-if" mode tests any crop sequence or water allocation.
- My farm records and a printable season report.
- Three detail levels (Simple, Moderate, Complete), so a farmer sees status words, key numbers and colours first, while an agronomist can see every number and source.

What we found on the demo field
- Continuous corn would have run short of water in 28 of 35 seasons under a 280 mm (11 in) allocation. No rotation removes the shortfall; the alternatives change when it happens and how big it is.
- Peak July corn demand (about 9.8 mm/day in 2026) exceeds what a 600 gpm well delivers on 50 ha (6.5 mm/day). The bottleneck is the well in July, not only the yearly allocation.
- 2026 had 38 days at or above 35 °C (95 °F) against a normal of 27.

How it works
- The analysis is ordinary JavaScript that runs in the visitor's browser on every visit, with no AI at runtime.
- It pulls this season's NASA POWER data live and recomputes everything with FAO-56 water-use methods, growing degree days, a root-zone water model built on USDA soil data, and percentiles against 1991–2020.
- A scheduled GitHub Action refreshes the stored history daily.
- A newly drawn field pulls 45 years of NASA data for its location in about 2 seconds.
- Farm records stay in the farmer's browser, with Export and Import.
- Tools: JavaScript (ES modules), Leaflet, Chart.js, Node.js precompute scripts, GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions.
